query: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Systematic thermal treatment using controlled variations in annealing temperature and cooling rate governs the phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs by directing the formation and stability of distinct phases.
generation.material_initial_state: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA in a homogenized or as-cast state exhibiting an initial mixture of phases
generation.intervention: Apply a series of controlled thermal cycles that vary the annealing temperature and cooling rate, with real‐time monitoring via in situ synchrotron X‐ray diffraction
generation.conditions: Experiments performed under controlled atmosphere conditions using repeated thermal cycles that span a range of annealing temperatures and cooling rates
generation.structural_mediator: The relative amounts of ordered (e.g., B2) versus disordered (e.g., BCC or FCC) phases, whose formation is sensitive to the applied thermal schedule
generation.mechanism: Controlled thermal energy input alters the kinetics and thermodynamics of phase nucleation and growth. By adjusting the thermal profile, the system can be driven towards metastable or equilibrium phases, while in situ XRD provides time-resolved structural feedback
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples will exhibit predictable alterations in phase fractions and microstructure; for example, higher annealing temperatures combined with rapid cooling may stabilize metastable phases, whereas lower temperatures or slower cooling may promote formation of equilibrium phases
generation.baseline: HEAs processed using conventional thermal methods without systematic control, which typically yield less predictable phase distributions
generation.boundary: The effect may be sensitive to slight compositional variations within the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni system and may not directly translate to other HEAs with different elemental makeups
generation.uncertainty: While the directional trends in phase control are expected, the precise quantitative effects of specific annealing temperatures and cooling rates require further experimental elucidation

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples and subject them to a controlled set of thermal treatments where the annealing temperature and cooling rate are systematically varied. Monitor phase evolution in situ using synchrotron XRD. Include control samples processed under standard thermal conditions without tailored cycling.
measurements: X-ray diffraction patterns to quantify phase fractions over time
Microstructural imaging (e.g., SEM, TEM) to observe morphological changes
Mechanical testing (e.g., hardness measurements) to correlate microstructural transitions with properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If controlled variations in annealing temperature and cooling rate do not produce statistically significant or reproducible differences in phase evolution compared to the control, or if in situ XRD does not capture the anticipated gradual phase transitions, the hypothesis would be falsified.

First reported in 2004 [ [1] ], high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys comprising five or more elements in equal or nearly equal molar fractions, with each element present at a mole fraction of approximately 5–35 at.% [ [2] ]. The presence of multiple elements leads to a high configurational entropy, resulting in solid-solution structures with face-centred cubic (FCC) and body-centred cubic (BCC) lattices, rather than intermetallic compounds [ [3] ]. In recent years, HEAs have garnered significant consideration in the field of materials science because of their exceptional performance characteristics, including high strength [ [4] ], corrosion resistance [ [5] ], soft magnetic properties [ [6] ], high hardness [ [7] ], wear resistance [ [8] ], fatigue resistance [ [9] ], and softening resistance at high temperatures [ [10] ]. The superior high-temperature behaviour of HEAs can be attributed to four underlying effects: the high entropy effect, the sluggish kinetic diffusion effect, the severe lattice distortion effect, and the cocktail effect [ [11] ].

In this paper, the impact of mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) on the phase evolution and mechanical properties development of CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloys (HEAs) was investigated. The microstructure and properties of the material were examined, using X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for surface morphology observation, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural analysis, and hardness testing to evaluate mechanical performance. The milled powder exhibited nanocrystalline solid solution microstructure with grain sizes below 48 nm, composed of 83% face–centered cubic (FCC) and 17% body–centered cubic (BCC) phases. Mechanically, the bulk CoCrFeNiTi alloy exhibited exceptional strength attributes, as evidenced by a Vickers hardness value reaching 675 Hv, along with a compressive strength of 1894 MPa and a yield stress of 1238 MPa.
